result.abstractText: The interaction between arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and phosphorus (P) availability could enhance plant drought tolerance. Yet whether this interaction modulates nutrient uptake and grain yield in oat by reshaping rhizosphere metabolite and microbial networks remains unresolved. A pot experiment was conducted across three relative water contents (75%, 55%, and 35% relative water content, designated WW, MDS, and SDS), two AMF treatments, and three P levels (0, 40, and 80 mg kg-¹ soil, designated P0, P1, and P2). Untargeted metabolomics and metagenomics were applied to characterize rhizosphere metabolite profiles and bacterial community structure, and to assess their relationships with nitrogen (N) and P status in the plant-soil system, grain yield and β-glucan. Drought significantly reduced grain yield, whereas moderate drought increased β-glucan accumulation; the beneficial effects of AMF on both traits were strongly modulated by soil P level. Under drought, AMF inoculation and P addition synergistically promoted N and P accumulation across oat organs; relative to P0AMF, P2AMF significantly elevated total N and P concentrations in roots, stems, leaves, panicles, and grains. Water availability was the dominant driver of rhizosphere metabolome and bacterial community variation. Under drought, AMF-P interaction further enriched rhizosphere metabolites, including amino acids and derivatives, organic acids, and benzene and substituted derivatives, while shifting the signature bacterial taxa toward Pseudomonadota (P1AMF) and Myxococcota and Gemmatimonadota (P2AMF). Network analysis identified isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) as a highly connected hub metabolite, exhibiting the strongest associations with N and P nutrition, grain yield, β-glucan, and bacterial community composition. Exogenous IPP application significantly increased oat plant height, stem dry weight, and average root diameter under drought and markedly elevated the relative abundances of several rhizosphere bacterial taxa. Collectively, these findings indicate that AMF inoculation combined with P addition is associated with restructuring of the rhizosphere metabolite-microbe network under drought, and that IPP represents a candidate metabolite that warrants further investigation in these plant-microbe-soil interactions. This study provides a correlative framework linking this dual strategy to shifts in rhizosphere microbial communities and crop yield and functional quality under water-limited conditions, although mechanistic validation will require future experimental work.

result.abstractText: The large grove-forming ectomycorrhizal tropical tree Microberlinia bisulcata displays strong mast fruiting on poor soils. Evidence is presented that masting is probably determined primarily by mineral nutrients and secondarily by radiation. To test the nutrient resource limitation hypothesis, phenological recordings were matched with climate variables and modelled using logistic time-series regression. A strong predictor was average daily rainfall in the dry season, low in the current year of masting and high in the year prior. Less strong was the increase in dry season radiation between prior and mast years. Masting events showed no relationship to annual stem increment. Masting intensity was reduced after two caterpillar attacks. Fallen-leaf phosphorus concentration increased in the inter-mast interval, and that for potassium peaked mid-interval. A drier dry season prior to masting may have increased tree carbon, while a wetter one increased nutrient uptake by roots and mycorrhizas. A rooting-fruiting trade-off in carbon is suggested. The long-term stochastic driver appears to be dry season rainfall. Synchrony across masting trees may be enhanced by equilibration of nutrients across the mycorrhizal-root network. A life-history strategy determined by mineral nutrient resource dynamics provides the best explanation and advanced model of the observed pattern of events.
